name: Plan B Dispatch
one_liner: A browser-native last-mile dispatcher: a hand-rolled ALNS solver running in Web Workers plans Solomon VRPTW fleets to best-known quality, then re-routes a mid-day van breakdown and five new orders in under two seconds, racing "quick repair" against "full re-solve" live on a glowing deck.gl mission-control map. Zero backend, zero API keys, zero cold start.
why_it_wins:
Contrarian read of the field. All four scouts converge on 4.2, so every strong team that reads the brief the same way lands there; 4.3 is the problem the organisers marked ★★★ and the one teams avoid because "dynamic re-planning scares them" and "OR-Tools needs a Python backend". Both reasons evaporate with parallel coding agents and a browser-only solver, which means a complete, polished 4.3 entry is almost certainly the only complete ★★★ submission in the room. A judge remembers the team that shipped the hardest problem end-to-end, not the third-best warehouse.

Three things make a judge lean forward. (1) An external truth: must-have 1 asks for distance against SINTEF's best-known results, so the first number on screen is "R101.25: 8 vehicles / 617.1 vs best-known 8 / 617.1, gap 0.0%" (or whatever the honest gap is). No other problem on the sheet has a published optimum to be measured against; 4.2's scores are internal and judges cannot calibrate them. (2) The algorithm is the visual: pressing "Breakdown van 3" makes the fleet visibly re-organise itself on a dark glowing map while two convergence curves race (repair finishes in ~200 ms, full re-solve in 2 s) and KPI tiles count the disruption cost. The "wow" is literally the core challenge being met live, so every hour of polish is also an hour on the must-have. (3) Nothing can fail on stage: the whole product is a static Vite site; the solver, simulator and renderer run in the judge's own browser tab, no tiles, no LLM rate limits, no Render cold start, deterministic seeds printed on screen.

Depth an expert recognises: a correct rolling-horizon formulation (vans start mid-arc with projected positions and remaining capacity, completed stops frozen), a pickup-at-breakdown rescue node with precedence so other vans physically collect the stranded parcels (the deepest Q&A probe, answered by construction), soft time windows with a lateness penalty so "late deliveries" is a real KPI rather than always zero, prize-collecting new orders so "orders not served" is reported instead of crashing, and a measured repair-vs-re-solve trade-off over 10 seeded scenarios, which is the PS's own stretch goal delivered as core. Indian logistics judges (Delhivery/Ecom Express/Swiggy-style last mile) recognise the problem instantly. Honest caveat vs 4.2: 4.2 is also under-picked and inherently 3D; 4.3 wins on external credibility, ambition signal and demo narrative, and its risk (solver correctness) is one that unit tests and seeded scenarios control, whereas 4.2's risk (GPU on the venue laptop/projector) is not fully in our hands.
demo_script:
Setup: deployed URL open in Chrome at 125% zoom on the dark theme, scenario link pre-loaded (?inst=R101.25&seed=7), backup MP4 on two laptops. One narrator, one operator; a judge is invited to press the event buttons.

0:00–0:25 Hook (slide 2 then switch to app). "Every fleet plans at 08:00. By 09:30 a van is dead on the flyover and five new orders have landed. Plan B Dispatch re-plans from where the vans actually are, within seconds, and tells you what the disruption cost." Point at the banner: "Solomon R101 benchmark, 25 customers, Euclidean units, synthetic street backdrop."

0:25–1:05 Must-have 1, WOW 1 "watch it think". Operator presses Solve. The solver-race panel shows the ALNS best-cost curve dropping in real time (~1.5 s); on the map the routes untangle live every 250 ms as improvements arrive (route-morph transitions), then draw themselves outward from the depot. KPI tiles count up: 8 vehicles, 617.1 distance; a badge appears: "Best known (SINTEF/Kohl et al.): 8 / 617.1, gap 0.0%" (the badge prints whatever the true gap is). Narrator: "Hand-written adaptive large-neighbourhood search, 600 lines of TypeScript, running in a Web Worker in your tab; nothing on a server."

1:05–1:50 Must-have 2 setup. Press Play at 20×. Vans glide along routes with fading light trails (TripsLayer), customer dots flip green as served, the Gantt strip fills row by row with time-window shading, the clock reads 08:00 + t. Scrub the timeline back and forth to show the state model is time-indexed (vans interpolate mid-arc).

1:50–3:05 WOW 2 "Breakdown at 09:30". Judge presses Breakdown van 3 at t=90. Red radial pulse at the van; its 4 remaining stops turn amber and detach with dashed links to a new "rescue" box at the breakdown point. Two workers start simultaneously: the race panel shows Repair converging in ~180 ms and Full re-solve in 2.0 s; old routes fade to dashed ghosts, new routes morph in. Van 1 visibly swings past the breakdown point to collect parcels before serving the orphans (precedence enforced). Disruption tiles count: distance +X, late deliveries N (total minutes), orders not served 0, stops that changed vehicle M. Toggle "show alternative" to overlay the losing strategy's plan. Narrator: "Completed stops are frozen, vans start where they are, parcels are physically transferred; soft windows after the disruption so we report lateness instead of hiding it."

3:05–3:45 WOW 3 "+5 orders, one honestly refused". Judge presses New orders at t=110: five pins (customers 26–30 of the 100-customer R101 parent, real benchmark windows) drop in with a transition. Re-plan runs; four are stitched in; one shows "not served: window closes at t=xxx, nearest van ETA t=yyy", with its drop penalty visible in the objective. Nothing is hidden.

3:45–4:20 Evidence tab. Table 1: C101.25 / R101.25 / RC101.25 (+ C102, R102, RC102) vehicles, distance, best-known, gap %, solver seconds, seed. Table 2: 10 seeded scenarios × 3 instances: Repair vs Full re-solve, mean ± sd of re-plan ms, cost delta, late, dropped, stability. Limitations line read aloud: Euclidean units, no road network or traffic, speed 1 unit/min, parcel-transfer assumption, penalties λ and π stated.

4:20–4:45 Stretch. Switch instance to R101 (100 customers), Solve: routes untangle for ~8 s, gap printed honestly. Show the driver QR; a teammate's phone shows "Van 1: next stop #17, ETA 10:04".

4:45–5:00 Close: repo, live URL, DEV_LOG, team names and who owns which module. Q&A cards ready: cargo transfer, soft vs hard windows, gap source, determinism, what breaks it.
wow_visual:
Rendering: deck.gl 9.4.0 with OrthographicView (COORDINATE_SYSTEM.CARTESIAN) directly on Solomon coordinates, no MapLibre, no tiles, so there is no Wi-Fi dependency and no dishonest "real city" implication. Dark mission-control theme (Tailwind 4.3.3 tokens), projector-safe: 3 px minimum line widths, 14 px+ labels, high-contrast per-van palette (8 vans max on 25-customer, 20 on 100-customer, colours from a fixed categorical ramp).

Layers (all data-driven from the single plan/state store, zustand 5.0.15):
1. Backdrop: a procedural street grid (LineLayer, 6% alpha) and random block footprints (PolygonLayer, 4% alpha) generated once from the seed, labelled "synthetic backdrop" in the banner.
2. Customers: ScatterplotLayer, radiusMinPixels 6, fill by status (pending slate, served green, late red, orphan amber, new order cyan, dropped grey with X icon via IconLayer); hover tooltip shows id, demand, window, planned arrival.
3. Routes: PathLayer per van, 3 px, plus a 9 px 20%-alpha copy underneath for glow; `transitions: {getPath: 600}` for morphing when vertex counts match, otherwise opacity cross-fade between an outgoing and incoming PathLayer; old plan kept as dashed ghost via PathStyleExtension (dashArray [4,3]).
4. Self-drawing routes on first solve: a TripsLayer whose timestamps are cumulative route distance; `currentTime` tweened 0 → max over 1.2 s so routes grow outward from the depot.
5. Vans: ScatterplotLayer heads (radiusMinPixels 7) positioned by the same projectState(plan, t) the re-planner uses, with a TripsLayer trail (trailLength 30 time units, fadeTrail true, widthMinPixels 4) so motion leaves glowing light.
6. Events: breakdown pulse = ScatterplotLayer whose radius is 8 + 6·sin(performance.now()/150) px via updateTriggers; rescue node = IconLayer box; amber LineLayer links from rescue node to each orphan until re-planned; new orders drop in with a getPosition transition from +8 units above.
7. Live solver preview: during the full re-solve, the worker posts its incumbent every 250 ms and the PathLayer morphs, so the fleet visibly untangles while the cost curve falls.

Panels: (a) Solver race: two best-cost-vs-ms lines (ECharts 6.1.0 line series, animationDurationUpdate 50) with iteration and ms counters, winner badge; (b) KPI tiles with counting numbers (motion 14.5.0 `animate(from,to)`): vehicles, distance, best-known & gap, late count/minutes, unserved, re-plan ms, stability; (c) Gantt strip (ECharts custom series): one row per van, segments for travel/wait/service, translucent time-window spans, late arrivals red, a moving clock cursor; (d) Timeline slider with play/pause and 1×/20×/60× speed; (e) Event log with timestamps and per-event KPI deltas plus "copy scenario link" (URL-encoded instance, seed, events) for reproduction; (f) Benchmark tab rendering bench/*.csv; (g) Driver view at ?driver=N (phone layout: next stop, ETA, remaining list) with a client-side QR code. A quality toggle disables glow copies and trails for weak GPUs; pixel ratio capped at 1.5; on-demand redraw outside playback.
wow_technical:
Core 1, static solver (must-have 1): Solomon I1 insertion construction (seed = farthest unrouted customer; α1=1, α2=0, λ=1) followed by Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search after Ropke & Pisinger (2006): destroy operators random, worst (highest detour cost, randomised power p=3), Shaw/related (distance + window + demand similarity, p=6) and whole-route removal (drives vehicle minimisation); repair operators greedy best-insertion, regret-2 and regret-3 with ±noise on insertion cost; simulated-annealing acceptance with T0 set so a 5%-worse solution is accepted with probability 0.5 and cooling 0.9995/iteration; adaptive operator weights with scores σ=(33,9,13), reaction factor 0.1, segments of 100 iterations; q ∈ [0.1n, 0.4n]. Objective for the benchmark is lexicographic (vehicles first) encoded as 10000·K + D with hard windows and capacity; route feasibility by O(n) time propagation (n ≤ 30 for the MVP; forward time slack, Savelsbergh 1992, as the 100-customer optimisation). Seeded PRNG (mulberry32), seed shown in the UI. Metric that proves it: vehicles and distance vs the published best-known / proven-optimal 25-customer values (C101.25 3/191.3, R101.25 8/617.1, RC101.25 4/461.1, C102.25 3/190.3, R102.25 7/547.1, RC102.25 3/351.8; Kohl et al. 1999 via SINTEF), gap % and seconds, over 10 seeds (mean, best, worst).

Core 2, rolling-horizon re-planning (must-have 2, the actual problem): projectState(plan, t) classifies every stop as served (departure ≤ t, frozen), in-service (arrival ≤ t < departure; van available at departure at that location) or free; a van between stops is placed by linear interpolation along its current arc with earliest availability t; remaining capacity = Q − delivered demand. The reduced problem gives each active van a virtual start node at its projected position and ready time, the real depot as end node with the depot's due time hard, and the free customers as required stops. Events: (a) breakdown of van b at t: b is removed from the fleet, its unserved stops become orphans, and a rescue node R_b at the breakdown point (service = 5 units, window [t, depot due]) is added with the precedence rule "any route serving an orphan must visit R_b before its first orphan"; load at R_b increases by the demand of the orphans that route takes, so capacity is checked at the pickup; several vans may each visit R_b (split pickup, stated assumption). Insertion of an orphan into a route lacking R_b evaluates the best joint insertion (R_b at any earlier position), O(n²) per attempt, fine for n ≤ 30. (b) 5 new orders = customers 26–30 of the 100-customer parent instance with their real windows, modelled prize-collecting (required=false, drop penalty π=1000), so an infeasible window yields "not served" with the reason displayed instead of an infeasible model. After a disruption, windows become soft with lateness penalty λ=2 per unit so late deliveries are counted; objective = remaining distance + λ·lateness + π·unserved (λ, π are sliders with stated defaults).

Core 3, two strategies measured head-to-head (PS stretch goal "compare full re-solve vs quick local repair", delivered as core): Repair = keep the projected assignments, regret-2 insert orphans and new orders (joint with the rescue node), then a 200 ms ALNS polish with small q biased to affected routes; Full re-solve = discard assignments, I1 from the vans' virtual starts, 2000 ms ALNS. Both run concurrently in two Web Workers streaming incumbents; the dispatcher applies the better objective (tie → repair for stability). KPIs per event: re-plan ms (each), disruption cost = new total planned cost − pre-event plan cost, late deliveries (count, minutes), orders not served, rescue detour distance, and stability = stops that changed vehicle. The bench script runs 10 seeded scenarios × 3 test instances headless with iteration budgets (deterministic) and emits CSV with mean ± sd; the README table is that CSV at a stated commit hash.

Why it is non-trivial: the state model (mid-arc projection, frozen prefixes, remaining capacity), the precedence-constrained rescue pickup, the switch from hard to soft windows with penalties, prize-collecting insertion, and operator adaptivity are each places where naive implementations silently produce infeasible or absurd plans; vitest invariants (delivered + remaining demand = total; no route visits an orphan before R_b; hard constraints never violated in static mode; served stops never move) make the correctness visible. Human explainability: ~600 lines across instance.ts, evaluate.ts, construct.ts, alns.ts, replan.ts; docs/solver.md holds the one-page pseudo-code each teammate studies for Q&A.
mvp_mapping:
Must-have 1 (static solver on a 25-customer Solomon instance with capacity and time windows, reporting vehicles and distance vs SINTEF best-known): public/instances/0025_C101.txt, 0025_R101.txt, 0025_RC101.txt (adzen mirror format: capacity, n, then id x y demand ready due service) parsed by src/core/instance.ts; src/core/construct.ts (Solomon I1) + src/core/alns.ts solve with hard windows, capacity and the lexicographic objective in a Web Worker (src/workers/solver.worker.ts); src/core/static.ts compares against bench/bks.json (values with Wayback source URLs and the Kohl et al. 1999 citation) and the UI shows vehicles, distance, best-known, gap % and seconds on the KPI tiles and in the Benchmark tab; `npm run bench:static` reproduces the table over 10 seeds.

Must-have 2 (event simulator with a clock injecting 5 new orders at a chosen time and one vehicle breakdown, re-planning from current state and reassigning the broken van's remaining stops): src/sim/clock.ts (continuous Solomon time units, play/pause/scrub, 1×/20×/60×), src/sim/state.ts projectState(plan, t) (served/in-service/free, mid-arc positions, remaining capacity), src/sim/events.ts (newOrders(t, ids 26–30 from the 100-customer parent), breakdown(t, van)), src/sim/replan.ts builds the reduced problem (virtual van starts, rescue node with precedence, soft windows, prize-collecting new orders) and runs Repair and Full re-solve in two workers, returning the new plan plus per-event KPIs; the broken van's stops are reassigned via the rescue-node pickup; an event log records each injection with its KPI deltas; `npm run bench:dynamic` replays 10 seeded scenarios headless.

Must-have 3 (deployed dispatcher dashboard: routes on a 2D map, timeline slider, event buttons, before/after KPIs for distance, late deliveries, orders not served): Vite 8 + React 19 static site on Vercel Hobby (fallback Cloudflare Pages), deck.gl OrthographicView 2D map with routes, customers, vans and trails; timeline slider with play controls; buttons Solve, Play, Breakdown van N (van picker), New orders, Reset, plus λ/π sliders; KPI tiles show pre-event vs post-event distance, late deliveries (count and minutes), orders not served, re-plan ms for both strategies and stability; ghost overlay of the previous plan; Gantt strip; copy-scenario-link for reproduction. Zero backend, so the public URL is live from hour 2 (walking skeleton) and cannot cold-start.
stretch_goals: Scale to 100-customer instances (C101, R101, RC101 from iRB-Lab/py-ga-VRPTW mirror; C101.sol best-known 10 / 827.3 under the DIMACS convention) with forward-time-slack feasibility and a 10 s budget; print the honest gap.

Full re-solve vs quick repair comparison with a 10-seed × 3-instance table (already core); extend with a third strategy (repair then full re-solve as background improvement that swaps in only if it beats repair by >2%).
Driver-facing mobile view at ?driver=N with next stop, ETA and remaining list; QR code on the pitch slide; phone layout tested on Android Chrome.
Stability-aware re-planning: a 'max stops that may change vehicle' knob with a penalty term, showing the cost of operational calm.
Cascading events: second breakdown or a late-arriving batch of orders; event log becomes a replayable timeline encoded in the URL.

Offline reference solutions with PyVRP 0.14.1 (HGS) via pyvrp.read(path, round_func="dimacs") so the README table shows BKS, HGS-5s and our ALNS side by side (Python run once on a laptop, nothing deployed).
Manhattan-distance mode snapping Solomon points to the synthetic street grid (clearly labelled as a visual variant, benchmark comparisons stay Euclidean).
Projector mode and colour-blind-safe palette toggle.
data_plan:
Dataset: Solomon (1987) VRPTW benchmark, public academic instances, no licence text; attribution: M. M. Solomon, "Algorithms for the Vehicle Routing and Scheduling Problems with Time Window Constraints", Operations Research 35(2), 1987; SINTEF TOP VRPTW pages (sintef.no/projectweb/top/vrptw/) for the benchmark description and best-known values; N. Kohl, J. Desrosiers, O. Madsen, M. Solomon, F. Soumis (1999) "2-Path Cuts for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows", Transportation Science 33(1), for the proven-optimal 25-customer values; Google OR-Tools VRPTW guide cited as the PS's suggested reference even though we do not use OR-Tools at runtime.

Files already on disk (data scout, verified 21 Oct 21:57 IST): _data/4.3/0025_C101.txt (583 B), 0025_R101.txt (551 B), 0025_RC101.txt (556 B) from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adzen/VRPTW/master/problems/0025_{C101,R101,RC101}.txt (line 1 capacity 200, line 2 n=25, then tab-separated id x y demand ready due service; depot id 0; e.g. R101 depot (35,35) due 230); 100-customer originals in Solomon format from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iRB-Lab/py-ga-VRPTW/master/data/text/{C101,R101,RC101}.txt (7.3–7.5 KB each) used for new orders (customers 26–30) and the 100-customer stretch; C101.txt + C101.sol from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PyVRP/VRPLIB/main/tests/data/ (10 routes, 827.3). The 25-customer instance is, by SINTEF's definition, the first 25 customers of the 100-customer file; the parser asserts the adzen 25-customer files equal that truncation. All instances (<10 KB each) are committed under public/instances/ with a fetch script scripts/fetch_instances.sh for provenance. SINTEF itself returns a Cloudflare 403 to scripts; a human opens the 25-customer page in a normal browser tonight to screenshot the table for docs/bks_source.png.

Best-known table committed as bench/bks.json with source URLs (Wayback copies of Solomon's tables: https://web.archive.org/web/2008id_/http://web.cba.neu.edu/~msolomon/c1c2solu.htm, r1r2solu.htm, rc12solu.htm): C101.25 3/191.3, C102.25 3/190.3, C104.25 3/186.9, C201.25 2/214.7, R101.25 8/617.1, R102.25 7/547.1, R103.25 5/454.6, R104.25 4/416.9, R105.25 6/530.5, R201.25 4/463.3, RC101.25 4/461.1, RC102.25 3/351.8, RC105.25 4/411.3, RC201.25 3/360.2; 100-customer C101 10/827.3, R101 20/1637.7, RC101 15/1619.8. Rounding convention stated: we compute double-precision Euclidean distances and report totals to one decimal (the SINTEF 25-customer convention); the DIMACS .sol convention (×10 truncation) differs by ≤0.2%, noted where the 100-customer .sol is used.

Preprocessing: none beyond parsing; time units are Solomon units with speed 1 unit per time unit; the UI clock maps 08:00 + t minutes for R/RC (horizon 230–240) and shows raw units for C-instances (horizon 1236). New orders use the parent instance's real coordinates, demand and windows.

Held-out evaluation (optimisation analogue of a test split): ALNS hyperparameters (q range, T0 rule, cooling, operator weights, noise) are tuned only on the dev instances C101.25 and R102.25; the test set is R101.25, RC101.25, C102.25, RC102.25 (+ the 100-customer trio for the stretch), reported over 10 seeds with mean/best/worst gap. Dynamic: bench/scenarios.json (10 seeds × 3 test instances; each scenario fixes the new-orders time, the breakdown time and the broken van drawn from the seed) is committed before any replan.ts tuning (target 23:30 IST, tagged eval-frozen) and results come only from `npm run bench:dynamic` with iteration budgets so numbers are deterministic; interactive demo runs use time budgets and say so. The demo scenario (R101.25, seed 7) is one of the 10 and is labelled "chosen for legibility" in the UI.
architecture:
Everything runs in the browser; the deployment is a static Vite 8 build on Vercel Hobby (fallback Cloudflare Pages; both zero cold start, no functions, no env vars; .env.example still shipped with a comment that no secrets are required).

Components:
1. src/core (pure TypeScript, no DOM): instance.ts (parsers for adzen 25-customer and Solomon 100-customer formats, truncation to first N), model.ts (types: Customer, Vehicle, Route, Plan, Problem incl. virtual starts, optional customers, precedence pairs), evaluate.ts (distance matrix as Float64Array, O(n) time propagation, lateness and capacity, objective), construct.ts (Solomon I1), alns.ts (destroy/repair/SA/adaptive weights, seeded mulberry32, iteration or time budget, progress callback), static.ts (benchmark run + BKS comparison).
2. src/sim: clock.ts, state.ts (projectState), events.ts, replan.ts (reduced-problem builder, Repair and Full strategies, KPIs, stability), scenarios.ts.
3. src/workers/solver.worker.ts: plain postMessage protocol {solve | replan, problem, budget, seed} → streams {incumbent, cost, iter, ms} every 50–250 ms and a final result; two workers are instantiated for the race. No Comlink, so the protocol is 40 explainable lines.
4. src/store (zustand 5.0.15): instance, plan, clock t, event log, KPI history, settings (λ, π, quality toggle, speed); a single source of truth read by the map, Gantt, tiles and driver view.
5. src/ui: DeckMap.tsx (deck.gl OrthographicView via @deck.gl/react 9.4.0, layers built from the store), Timeline.tsx, EventButtons.tsx, KpiTiles.tsx, SolverRace.tsx (ECharts), Gantt.tsx (ECharts custom series), EventLog.tsx, BenchmarkTab.tsx (renders bench/*.csv bundled at build), DriverView.tsx (?driver=N), Banner.tsx (honesty banner).
6. bench/: run_static.ts and run_dynamic.ts executed with tsx under Node, importing the same src/core and src/sim modules (no browser), writing bench/results_static.csv and bench/results_dynamic.csv with commit hash and date; `npm run bench` runs both; CI (GitHub Actions) runs vitest + bench on every push to main so README numbers are reproducible.
7. docs/: architecture.md (Mermaid), solver.md (one-page ALNS pseudo-code), replan.md (state model, rescue node, penalties), bks_source.png, demo/script.md, pitch/PlanB_NexAI2026.pptx (python-pptx).

Data flow: instance file → parser → Problem → worker (ALNS) → Plan → store → (map layers, Gantt, tiles). Clock tick → projectState(plan, t) → van positions for rendering (same function the re-planner uses). Event button → events.ts → replan.ts builds reduced Problem → two workers → incumbents stream to SolverRace and (for full re-solve) to the map preview → final plans → apply better → KPIs → store → tiles/log. Scenario link encodes instance, seed, events in the URL so judges can reproduce.

Compute placement: solver and simulator in Web Workers (main thread stays at 60 fps); rendering on the GPU via deck.gl WebGL2; optional Python (PyVRP) runs only offline on a laptop for a README reference column. Nothing server-side.
stack: typescript 5.9.3 (pin the 5.x line; 7.0.2 is the new Go compiler, avoid for this build)
tsx (latest 4.x, pin after `npm view tsx version` tonight) for bench scripts
qrcode (npm, pin after `npm view qrcode version`) for the driver-view QR
Offline only, optional: Python 3.12, pyvrp 0.14.1, vrplib 2.2.0 (reference HGS solutions), python-pptx (pitch deck)
Hosting: Vercel Hobby static (fallback Cloudflare Pages Free); GitHub Actions for vitest + bench
build_plan:
Clock: now 21:30 IST 21 Oct; feature freeze 11:00 IST 22 Oct; submit by 14:45. Hour 0 = 21:45. Four coding agents in parallel on branches feat/solver, feat/dynamic, feat/scene, chore/rigor; a human merges to main at least every 45 minutes (hourly-commit rule) with meaningful messages; the first commit (README skeleton, .env.example, DEV_LOG.md noting 18:00–21:30 was planning, LICENSE MIT, .gitignore) lands by 21:50.

Hour 0–0.5 (all): Agent 1 publishes src/core/model.ts (shared types: Problem, Plan, Route, Event, KPI, worker message protocol) and a stub solver returning the I1 solution; everyone codes against it.

Agent 1 "Solver" (≈6 h, 0–6): instance parsers + assertion that 0025_* equals the first 25 customers of the 100-customer file; evaluate.ts; construct.ts (I1); alns.ts (operators, SA, adaptive weights, seeded PRNG, iteration/time budgets, progress callback); solver.worker.ts; static.ts + bench/run_static.ts; vitest: distance matrix, hand-computed 3-stop time propagation, capacity, I1 feasibility, ALNS never violates hard constraints, C101.25 reaches 3/191.3 within an iteration budget on ≥9/10 seeds (record the truth if not). Hour 4 checkpoint: static table vs BKS printed.

Agent 2 "Dynamic" (≈7 h, 0–7): clock.ts; state.ts projectState with invariants; events.ts; replan.ts (virtual starts, rescue node + precedence in insertion, soft windows, prize-collecting, Repair and Full strategies, KPIs, stability); scenarios.ts + bench/run_dynamic.ts; vitest: served stops frozen, orphans never before R_b, capacity at pickup, delivered + remaining = total demand, dropped order has a displayed reason. Uses the stub solver until Agent 1's ALNS lands (~hour 4), then swaps.

Agent 3 "Scene" (≈8 h, 0–8): Vite app, theme, DeckMap with OrthographicView and all layers against fixtures/plan_R101.json; self-drawing routes; van heads + trails from projectState; timeline; event buttons; KPI tiles with counting numbers; SolverRace panel; Gantt; EventLog + copy-link; BenchmarkTab; DriverView + QR; quality toggle; banner. Hour 2: walking skeleton deployed to Vercel (instance rendered, play works) for progress reviews.

Agent 4 "Rigor & Ship" (≈5 h, 0–3 then 9–11): scripts/fetch_instances.sh, bench/bks.json with sources, bench/scenarios.json frozen and tagged eval-frozen before any tuning (target 23:30), docs/solver.md and docs/replan.md, README sections per the judge checklist (problem, architecture Mermaid, stack table, setup, must-have checklist with file paths, data attribution, evaluation, limitations, AI-tools declaration, team), DEV_LOG template and hourly entries, GitHub Actions (vitest + bench), Vercel project, optional PyVRP reference run, demo script, pitch .pptx via python-pptx, LinkedIn/X drafts, backup-video checklist.

Integration and QA (≈4 h, hours 7–11, one agent + humans): wire scene to workers, replace fixtures, scripted demo scenario (R101.25 seed 7, breakdown t=90, new orders t=110) verified to produce legible late/dropped outcomes, performance on a 4-year-old laptop and at 1280×720 projector, Chrome + Edge, cross-check README numbers = bench CSV at the frozen commit, record the 5-min backup MP4 and 3-min YouTube cut, Q&A cards (10), assign every file to a named owner.

Totals ≈ 30 agent-hours over ≈ 11 wall-clock hours of agent work (21:45 → ~09:00), leaving 09:00–11:00 for polish and sleep-shifted humans, 11:00–12:30 final eval + README/DEV_LOG, 12:30–13:30 demo recording + deck, 13:30–14:15 posts, 14:15–14:45 smoke test on another laptop and phone, submit.
risks: ALNS misses the best-known value on a test instance (e.g. R101.25 617.1). Mitigation: the badge prints the true gap; iteration budget and the route-removal operator raise the hit rate; dev/test split keeps tuning honest; optional offline PyVRP column shows what HGS gets; the demo narrative never depends on 0.0%.

Re-planning state bugs (van mid-arc, capacity after partial delivery, orphan served before the rescue pickup). honesty_plan: Every number on screen is computed live from the committed instance files by the same code the bench script runs; the README tables are the output of `npm run bench` at a stated commit hash and date, and CI re-runs them on every push to main. Best-known values are cited with their source URLs (Wayback copies of Solomon's tables, SINTEF, Kohl et al. 1999) and the rounding convention is stated; the gap badge prints whatever the solver achieved, including misses. Hyperparameters are tuned only on dev instances (C101.25, R102.25) and reported on disjoint test instances over 10 seeds with mean/best/worst; the dynamic scenario file is committed and tagged eval-frozen before replan.ts is tuned, and the demo scenario is labelled as one of those ten. Both strategies' KPIs are always shown, including when repair loses, and "orders not served" and "late deliveries" are counted with the penalties (λ=2 per time unit, π=1000) printed next to them as adjustable sliders. Assumptions are written in the UI banner and README: Solomon coordinates in Euclidean units, no road network or traffic, speed 1 unit per time unit, synthetic street backdrop for legibility only, parcels physically transferred at the breakdown point with a 5-unit transfer time and split pickup allowed, soft windows only after a disruption, single depot, capacity only, no driver breaks, no LLM anywhere (the pitch says "heuristic optimisation", not "AI predicts"). PS watch-outs respected: distances are kept in floating point so no OR-Tools integer scaling is needed and we say why; the solver has a visible time or iteration budget (≤ 2 s re-plan, 5 s static) so re-planning stays interactive; nothing is copied from the OR-Tools sample, and the re-planning formulation is documented as the centre of the work. Limitations section lists what would change on real roads (asymmetric travel times, traffic, service-time variance) and states that 25-customer instances are small by industry standards. AI-tools declaration names Claude Code agents, how each module was reviewed by a named human, and the DEV_LOG records rejected approaches (OR-Tools backend on Render rejected for cold-start risk; MapLibre tiles rejected as misleading for synthetic coordinates).
